Loops are topographically organized cortico-subcortical-cortical circuits in which a cortical territory sends a copy of its state to a specialized subcortical module, that module transforms it according to its own objectives and learning rules, and thalamic or direct output returns the result to the same-or functionally allied-cortical field. Because different hubs optimize on different timescales and signals, the brain runs many such loops in parallel. The effect is to interleave evaluation (basal ganglia), prediction and timing (cerebellum), routing/attention and working-memory stabilization (thalamus), and episodic indexing and sequence generation (hippocampus) directly into ongoing cortical computation. Rather than a one-way pipeline, cortex operates inside a reentrant heterarchy where loop outputs continuously shape the next cortical step. A 2026 review maps cerebellar circuit architecture (Figure) 10. The review illustrates cerebellar functional loops (Figure).

Basal ganglia loops implement context-sensitive gating and policy learning: direct/indirect/hyperdirect channels regulate which motor or cognitive program is released, how vigorous it is, and when to withhold action under conflict. Dopamine conveys reward-prediction errors that retune corticostriatal synapses, solving temporal credit assignment with eligibility traces and, over repetition, compiling habits. Cerebello-cortical loops function as forward-model predictors and timing regulators. Their massively expanded granule cell code and climbing-fiber teaching signals support precise, millisecond-scale calibration of movements and, in association territories (e.g., Crus I/II), the automation and smoothing of cognitive sequences. The latest human subcortical connectome combines a loop schematic with a high-resolution tractography reconstruction of direct, indirect, and hyperdirect pathways (Figure) 8. Its tractography reconstructs motor and premotor basal ganglia pathways through putamen, pallidum, and thalamus (Figure). This recent anatomical atlas provides a detailed view of the pathways discussed here (Figure). This recent anatomical atlas provides a detailed view of the pathways discussed here (Figure).

Thalamo-cortical loops provide the brain’s dynamic I/O and coordination fabric. Core relays deliver precise feedforward drive while matrix-type nuclei (pulvinar, MD) send broad, layer-1 feedback that carries context, attention, and predictions. These bidirectional exchanges naturally implement predictive-coding style computations-gamma-dominated feedforward channels emphasize unexpected input; alpha/beta-dominated feedback carries priors and top-down suppression-while MD<->PFC circuits stabilize delay activity for working memory and flexibly set decision thresholds. Hippocampo-cortical loops supply the complementary memory operations: dentate/CA3 separate overlapping inputs and complete sparse cues; theta sequences and ripple-time replay generate and evaluate prospective or past trajectories; repeated replay trains long-term cortical schemas.

Across systems, the common motif is a reentrant transform-and-return: cortex proposes, specialized modules evaluate/predict/index on their preferred objective and timescale, and the refined signal re-enters cortex to update perception, cognition, and action. This architecture yields three system-level advantages. First, it distributes learning across mechanisms tuned to different feedback (dopamine RPEs, climbing-fiber errors, cortico-thalamic context), improving sample efficiency and robustness. Second, it enforces flexible control-global "stops" and local "goes," attentionally gated routing, and stability of task sets when needed. Third, it supports multi-horizon computation: cerebellar timing (ms), thalamo-cortical maintenance (hundreds of ms to seconds), basal-ganglia policy shaping (seconds to days), and hippocampal consolidation (hours to years). In short, loops are the brain’s integration pattern: the reason evaluation, prediction, memory, and action selection stay coupled yet modular, giving biological agents both speed and adaptivity.

More on these specific loops in the in Systems-Level Architecture section. Covering thalamo-cortical loops here since they show up in every subsystem.

Thalamocortical architectures for flexible cognition and efficient learning

A thalamocortical circuit encoding deviations from sensory history

Thalamo-Cortical Loops

Thalamo-cortical loops are recurrent circuits connecting the thalamus and cerebral cortex, forming bidirectional pathways that underlie much of the brain’s information processing. Unlike many brain region interactions that are one-directional, the cortex and thalamus send massive excitatory projections to each other, engaging essentially all cortical areas and thalamic nuclei in loops. These loops have long been implicated in fundamental neural functions - from generating brain rhythms (sleep spindles, alpha oscillations) to enabling sensory attention and inter-areal communication. Historically, the thalamus was viewed as a simple relay for sensory signals, but modern evidence reveals a more complex, interactive architecture: specific thalamic nuclei connect with defined cortical layers and regions, and feedback from cortex profoundly modulates thalamic transmission.

Anatomy

Each thalamic nucleus has a reciprocal relationship with specific cortical areas, forming distinct thalamo-cortical loops. First-order (relay) nuclei (sometimes called core-type nuclei) receive direct sensory or subcortical input and project mainly to primary cortical areas. Examples include the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) for vision (projecting to V1), medial geniculate body (MGN) for audition (to A1), and ventrobasal complex (VB; comprising VPL/VPM) for somatosensation (to S1). These core nuclei typically project topographically to layer 4 of cortex and nearby layers, providing a focused, point-to-point relay of sensory information.

In contrast, higher-order (association) nuclei (often matrix-type nuclei) receive a significant driving input from cortex itself (via descending layer 5 pathways) and project more diffusely to higher cortical areas. Examples are the pulvinar and lateral posterior (LP) nuclei in visual systems (connecting to parietal and temporal cortex), the mediodorsal (MD) nucleus connecting with prefrontal cortex, and the ventral medial (VM) nucleus connecting with frontal premotor areas. These matrix-type nuclei tend to project to superficial cortical layers (layers 1 and 2/3) over broad areas, often influencing apical dendrites of pyramidal neurons and coordinating activity across cortical regions 3. A 2026 review diagrams transthalamic pathways (Figure) 9. The review describes divergent thalamic projections (Figure).

Thalamo-cortical loops are usually named by the corresponding thalamic nucleus and its cortical target. For example, the visual loop comprises retina -> LGN -> visual cortex (V1) -> back to LGN; the auditory loop involves cochlea -> MGN -> auditory cortex; and a somatosensory loop links dorsal column nuclei -> VPL/VPM -> somatosensory cortex. Importantly, association loops connect higher-order thalamic nuclei with frontal and parietal cortices; for instance, the mediodorsal (MD) thalamus <-> prefrontal cortex (PFC) loop and pulvinar <-> visual association cortex loops are critical for cognition and attention. Beyond sensory pathways, the thalamus also participates in motor and limbic loops: e.g. the ventrolateral (VL) thalamus relays signals from cerebellum and basal ganglia to motor cortex, closing a motor loop; the anterior and midline thalamic nuclei connect with cingulate and hippocampal regions, forming loops involved in memory and emotion. Thus, virtually every cortical area is part of a specific thalamic loop, underscoring that cortex and thalamus function as an integrated circuit rather than isolated processors.

Each loop exhibits reciprocal connectivity: the thalamic relay neurons send excitatory afferents to cortex, and in turn cortical neurons (primarily deep-layer pyramidal cells) send excitatory feedback projections back to those same thalamic neurons. This reciprocity creates a closed loop that can sustain reverberant activity. The feedforward (thalamo->cortical) pathway often carries rapidly time-locked information (e.g. a visual stimulus onset), while the feedback (cortico->thalamic) pathway can modulate the gain, context, or timing of thalamic relay, rather than simply echoing the input. Indeed, the feedback projections far outnumber the feedforward inputs in many cases: for example, in the LGN as little as  5-10% of synapses come from retinal fibers, whereas up to 95% of inputs are from cortical feedback, local GABAergic interneurons, the thalamic reticular nucleus, and brainstem modulatory systems. This anatomical fact highlights that the thalamus is not a passive relay - it is a convergence hub where cortical and subcortical signals intermingle to shape what is ultimately sent to cortex.

Within each cortical area, thalamic inputs and cortical outputs are arranged in a precise laminar pattern. Core-type thalamic neurons (often parvalbumin-positive in primates) project to the middle cortical layers (layer 4 and lower layer 3), forming dense terminal arbors often called "thalamo-recipient layers". These projections create the initial feedforward drive in cortical columns and also excite local inhibitory interneurons, producing feedforward inhibition that sharpens spatial and temporal response properties. Matrix-type thalamic neurons (often calbindin-positive) project more to layer 1 and upper layers (1-2), spreading more diffusely. A given cortical area can receive a mix of core and matrix inputs: for instance, primary visual cortex (V1) gets core input from LGN (to layer 4) and also matrix input from the pulvinar/LP (to layer 1). Higher-order association cortices (e.g. prefrontal, temporal) often receive predominantly matrix-type input to layer 1 from association thalamic nuclei like MD or pulvinar. The functional consequence is that core inputs deliver precise sensory details to cortical circuits, while matrix inputs provide a more modulatory, context-carrying signal to the distal dendrites of pyramidal neurons (in layer 1), influencing how cortex interprets or prioritizes information. The review discusses experimental tests of the pathway (Figure). The review illustrates candidate gating mechanisms (Figure).

From the cortical side, there are discrete classes of pyramidal cells that participate in thalamo-cortical loops. Layer 6 corticothalamic (CT) neurons project almost exclusively to the thalamus (with a collateral to the inhibitory thalamic reticular nucleus), and provide the main feedback pathway to first-order thalamic relays. These layer 6 cells typically make small, modulatory synapses on thalamic relay neurons and often target the distal dendrites, implying they modulate thalamic responsiveness rather than driving it strongly. Layer 5B pyramidal tract (PT) neurons, in contrast, are large output cells that send one branch down to subcortical structures (e.g. forming the corticospinal or corticopontine tracts) and another collateral branch up to higher-order thalamic nuclei 4. These layer 5->thalamus projections are thought to act as drivers for higher-order thalamic relays (like pulvinar, MD, LP, etc.), in a similar way that retinal afferents drive the LGN. Indeed, many higher-order thalamic nuclei essentially sit in between cortical areas: a PT neuron in one cortical area can send a driver signal to a thalamic nucleus, which then projects to another cortical area - forming a trans-thalamic cortico-cortical circuit. This provides an indirect route for cortical areas to influence each other via the thalamus (in addition to direct cortico-cortical fibers). Meanwhile, intratelencephalic (IT) neurons are the typical cortico-cortical pyramidal cells (located in layers 2/3, 5A and 6) that project within the cortex and to striatum, but notably do not project to the thalamus. IT cells instead form local recurrent networks and long-range cortical pathways. They help "close the loop" on the cortical side by integrating thalamic input and feeding activity back into deep layers or to other cortical regions. Importantly, IT neurons often mediate the connection between cortico-thalamo-cortical (CTC) loops and pure cortico-cortical (CC) circuits: they receive thalamic input and can broadcast it to other cortical areas. This means the thalamic loop doesn’t function in isolation - it’s interwoven with cortical networks via these IT neurons acting as hubs.

In summary, a "core loop" (first-order) might involve a layer 6 CT neuron projecting to a relay nucleus, which in turn projects to layer 4 of the same cortical area, and an IT neuron in layer 4/5 completes the loop by connecting back to layer 6 or locally. A "higher-order loop" might involve a layer 5 PT neuron driving a matrix-type thalamic nucleus, which projects broadly to layer 1 and 5A of higher cortical areas, and then IT neurons propagate that activity within cortex and perhaps back to layer 6 of the originating area. Researchers distinguish "simple" vs. "complex" CTC loops: simple loops consist of a direct reciprocal pair (one population of cortical neurons monosynaptically connected to one thalamic population), whereas complex loops include additional cortical interneurons or IT neurons that create multi-synaptic chains closing the loop. Many higher loops are complex, engaging a web of intracortical connections. Even within a single cortical area, multiple loop types may coexist (for example, S1 has a first-order loop via VPM and a higher-order loop via posterior thalamic nucleus PO).

Operation

A thalamo-cortical loop has distinct feedforward and feedback streams that together form a recurrent circuit. Feedforward flow generally refers to signals originating in the periphery or lower areas, ascending through the thalamus into cortex. For instance, when a visual stimulus appears, retinal ganglion cells fire -> LGN relay cells transmit bursts to V1 (layer 4) -> V1 neurons process and forward signals to higher visual cortices. Such ascending drive is often rapid and time-locked to stimuli, initiating cortical responses. Feedback flow denotes signals from cortex back to thalamus (and also from higher cortical areas back to lower ones). These descending signals can carry contextual information, predictions, or attention-related modulation. In the visual example, V1 sends axons back to LGN (mostly from layer 6 CT cells) and even higher visual areas send feedback to V1 and LGN (via higher-order thalamus like pulvinar). Feedback typically is not a simple mirror of feedforward content; instead it can sharpen or suppress certain inputs and synchronize thalamic neurons. In fact, corticothalamic fibers outnumber incoming drivers in many relays, and they terminate broadly (often on distal dendrites or inhibitory interneurons), consistent with a modulatory role.

This recurrent architecture allows iterative refinement of neural representations. A classic hypothesis by David Mumford (1991) suggested that each cortical area and its thalamic partner form a "comparison loop" that implements a form of predictive coding: the cortex sends an expectation of incoming features down to the thalamus, where it is compared with the actual incoming signal, and any mismatch (error) is sent back up to cortex. In this view, feedforward inputs carry error signals (novel or unpredicted information) while feedback conveys predictions or context, and the loop continually adjusts cortical activity to minimize error. Whether literally true or not, this concept aligns with the observation that cortico-thalamic feedback can suppress predictable inputs or amplify unexpected ones. For example, if an expected stimulus is suddenly omitted or altered, thalamic relay cells often respond with burst firing (due to a release from cortical inhibition) signaling a "surprise." Conversely, focused attention from cortex can pre-depolarize specific thalamic neurons, putting them in a tonic mode that relays information faithfully while filtering out irrelevant signals (see Attention and Gating below). Thus, information flow in the loop is bidirectional and dynamic: cortex influences what thalamus relays, and thalamus gates what cortex perceives. Hierarchical predictive coding passes messages in both directions. (Figure) 15. Predictive coding passes messages down and errors up. (Figure).

The directionality also maps onto distinct frequency channels. Fast oscillations (gamma  30-80 Hz) are often prominent in feedforward pathways (superficial cortical layers to thalamus and onward), whereas slower oscillations (alpha/beta  8-20 Hz) are seen in feedback (deep cortical layers projecting to thalamus). This spectral separation is thought to help organize the hierarchy: high-frequency synchronized bursts can drive the next stage, while lower-frequency rhythms convey contextual modulation. For instance, attending to a stimulus increases gamma coherence between LGN and V1 or between V1 and V4, tightening feedforward coupling, whereas feedback signals from higher areas to lower might ride on alpha oscillations associated with expectation or top-down suppression. Thalamo-cortical loops thus operate with a temporal coding scheme where feedforward and feedback streams interact but retain some distinction in timing and frequency domain 5. The net result is a loop that can resonate - supporting sustained activity (working memory states, oscillatory rhythms) - but also remain responsive to new inputs.

Functions

Sensory Relay and Preprocessing

At the most basic level, thalamo-cortical loops handle sensory signal transmission from the outside world to the cortex. But rather than a passive relay, the loop performs preprocessing such as filtering, sharpening, and timing control. The thalamus can emphasize novel or significant inputs by switching into burst mode for a transient, high-salience signal. It can also suppress transmission when appropriate: e.g. during sleep or inattention, strong TRN inhibition causes relay neurons to oscillate among themselves (spindles) rather than forwarding input to cortex. Even in waking, the thalamus contributes to adapting sensory processing. A classic example is the lateral geniculate nucleus in vision: LGN cells receive not just retinal input but also feedback from visual cortex and brainstem (e.g. locus coeruleus, dorsal raphe). This allows state-dependent gating - for instance, under high arousal, LGN throughput is increased (tonic mode, less surround inhibition), improving visual sensitivity, whereas under relaxed conditions, more surround inhibition or burst firing might enhance detection of only the most salient changes.

Additionally, receptive field properties of thalamic neurons can shape cortical responses. Many relay cells already exhibit center-surround organization (enhancing contrast), and some higher-order relays integrate inputs (e.g. the pulvinar integrates signals from superior colliculus and cortex, potentially combining retinal and cortical motion information). Thus, the loop’s initial feedforward pass is a processed version of raw sensory data, conditioned by the organism’s internal state. The cortical side of the loop further sharpens tuning through intracortical circuits, but notably much of that sharpening involves thalamic input driving feedforward inhibition. For example, a whisker deflection in rodents triggers thalamic VB neurons that excite layer-4 fast-spiking interneurons in barrel cortex, which in turn laterally inhibit neighboring barrels - leading to a crisp spatial encoding of which whisker moved. This is an emergent property of the TC loop: only the connections present enable this computation (VB->PV interneuron->silence adjacent columns). If the thalamus simply broadcast uniformly, the specificity would be lost. Therefore, one computational role of TC loops is sensory feature selection and enhancement - highlighting important inputs and localizing them in space and time for the cortex.

Attention and Gating

Thalamo-cortical loops play a pivotal role in selective attention - dynamically gating the flow of sensory or cognitive information. The pulvinar (in visual and association loops) is often described as an "attentional spotlight" or hub that coordinates cortical areas. When attention is directed to a visual target, pulvinar neurons not only increase their firing rates but also synchronize their activity with the cortical circuits processing that target. By phase-aligning oscillations in those cortical areas, the pulvinar loop effectively boosts effective connectivity between them. The review summarizes candidate functions (Figure). An October 2026 human study targets thalamus with focused ultrasound (Figure) 11. The study tests central-thalamic stimulation (Figure). The study compares pulvinar and central-thalamic targets (Figure).

Attention-related gating is not unique to pulvinar. Modality-specific loops also exhibit attention modulation. In the LGN, when a subject attends to a visual stimulus, responses of LGN neurons to that stimulus are enhanced (an effect likely mediated by feedback from visual cortex and cholinergic basal forebrain inputs). Similarly, the MD thalamus in cognitive tasks can gate prefrontal cortex processing (discussed below). A unifying principle is that thalamo-cortical loops allow top-down signals to intervene at an early stage of processing.

Working Memory and Executive Loops

Growing evidence indicates that working memory - the temporary holding and manipulation of information - relies on thalamo-cortical loops, especially involving the mediodorsal (MD) thalamus and prefrontal cortex. Classical models of working memory often focused on persistent recurrent activity in cortical circuits alone (e.g. PFC maintaining a trace of a cue). However, recent optogenetic and electrophysiological studies in rodents show that disconnecting or silencing the MD thalamus profoundly disrupts PFC working memory function. In one study, during a spatial working memory task, MD->PFC activity was required to sustain persistent firing of PFC neurons during the memory delay, and inactivation of MD caused those delay-period representations to fade, leading to errors 6. Interestingly, the reverse pathway (PFC->MD) was needed later, at the choice period, suggesting a loop: the thalamus helps keep information online in cortex, and then the cortex instructs the thalamus when to clear or use that information for decisions. These findings paint the thalamus as an "amplifier" or stabilizer of cortical activity in service of working memory. Because the MD thalamus has diffuse connectivity with PFC (matrix-type projections to superficial layers and even to inhibitory interneurons), it is well-placed to influence network excitability.

Predictive Coding and Error Signaling

Predictive coding theories propose that the cortex constantly generates predictions of incoming sensory inputs and compares them with actual inputs, with only the mismatch (prediction error) being propagated forward. Thalamo-cortical loops have been hypothesized to implement this comparison and error gating. Classic ideas (Mumford, 1991; later Friston, 2010) envisioned the thalamus as an "active blackboard" where cortical feedback (predictions) are written and then updated by sensory input differences. Recent experimental evidence provides concrete examples of this principle in action. A 2024 study by Furutachi et al. demonstrated a circuit for prediction-error generation in mouse visual cortex that crucially involves the thalamus. When mice were trained to expect a certain visual pattern in a virtual reality setup, neurons in V1 responded normally if the pattern appeared as predicted. But if an unexpected stimulus appeared instead, a specific subset of V1 neurons (those tuned to the unexpected feature) showed a selectively boosted response, as if signaling "this feature was not predicted". This selective amplification of unpredicted input was traced to a cooperative thalamo-cortical disinhibitory circuit: the higher-order thalamus (the pulvinar/LP in this case) provided a supplementary input to V1 when the surprise occurred, and at the same time, VIP interneurons in V1 became active to silence SST interneurons, thereby lifting inhibition from the pyramidal cells that prefer the unexpected stimulus 7. In other words, breaking a prediction engaged a loop where the thalamus + local cortical circuit worked together to enhance the error signal (the unexpected feature). If either the thalamic input or the VIP interneuron activity was experimentally blocked, this selective amplification did not happen - showing that the thalamus was required for robust error signaling. The model proposes a biological mapping of message passing (Figure) 13. A 2026 model compares error-neuron microcircuits with predictive-coding networks (Figure) 14.

Another way to frame this is through active inference - the idea that the brain not only passively predicts but also takes actions to fulfill predictions (minimize surprise). Thalamo-cortical loops are positioned to influence action selection via their connections to motor circuits (basal ganglia, cerebellum loops) and to sensorimotor cortex. For example, the higher-order loops through the pulvinar and MD might signal when an outcome deviates from the internal model, and this could engage frontal-striatal circuits to adjust behavior. Some theories propose that the intralaminar thalamus (central lateral nucleus and others) broadcast prediction errors widely (as part of a "global workspace") to update multiple cortical areas and possibly drive exploratory behavior. While direct evidence for thalamic involvement in active inference is still emerging, the known anatomy fits: thalamic outputs reach broad cortical territories and can rapidly alter cortical states, which is what a global error broadcast or belief update requires. Notably, the anterior cingulate loop through midline thalamus might convey reward prediction errors or context changes that motivate policy shifts. In rodents, inactivating the medial thalamus impairs the ability to use contextual cues for behavior (which can be seen as a deficit in inferring the correct context). All these points converge on the idea that thalamo-cortical loops compute "differences" and "updates" - whether it’s sensory surprise, cognitive set shifting, or a violation of expectation, the loops kick in to signal the rest of the brain that an update is needed. This contrasts with the cortex alone, which might settle into a predictive state; the thalamus is a node that can inject a disruptive corrective signal when reality and prediction diverge.

Decision-Making and Action Selection

Thalamo-cortical loops are also integral to circuits that underlie decision-making. Here, the loops often involve interactions with the basal ganglia. A canonical pathway is the cortico-basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex loop, where cortex projects to striatum (input of BG), BG output nuclei (like GPi) inhibit thalamus, and thalamus projects back to cortex. The thalamus in these loops (e.g. ventroanterior and ventrolateral nuclei for motor, MD for executive) serves as the final gateway that either allows a cortical command to be executed or not, depending on BG disinhibition. Thus, one can think of the thalamus as the "gate that opens" when a decision is made - for example, when the basal ganglia decides to initiate a movement, it releases the VL thalamus from inhibition, and VL then drives motor cortex to generate the action. In decision tasks under uncertainty, cognitive thalamic loops also contribute. We saw earlier that MD has distinct circuits for handling uncertainty (low signal vs high noise). In practical terms, during a difficult decision with conflicting evidence, the thalamus might dampen impulsive cortical activity (via one pathway) until enough signal accumulates, and then amplify the chosen direction’s cortical ensemble (via another pathway) once confidence is higher. Animal studies support this: if MD is lesioned, animals often have decision-making deficits, such as being unable to adjust choices based on changing rules or probabilities (they perseverate or get distracted easily). This mirrors PFC lesions, suggesting the loop as a whole is required. A recent striatal model links dopamine-dependent plasticity and direct/indirect pathway activity to action selection and reinforcement learning (Figure) 12. A recent striatal model links dopamine-dependent plasticity and direct/indirect pathway activity to action selection and reinforcement learning (Figure).

Another intriguing role is in active sensing: the thalamo-cortical circuits (particularly those involving higher-order thalamus and layer 5 PT neurons) might help decide where to sample information next. For instance, the circuit from frontal eye field (FEF) cortex -> thalamus (pulvinar or MD) -> back to visual cortices could influence where to move the eyes by highlighting particular stimuli. Some experiments in primates show that microstimulating the thalamus can bias choices or attention, indicating a causal role in guiding decisions. There is also emerging evidence that thalamic loops contribute to conscious decision processes. The central lateral thalamus has been called a "higher-order state" nucleus that might reflect the current rule or plan and broadcast it (some have tied this to conscious awareness of actions). While these ideas are still speculative, it’s clear that beyond sensory gating, the thalamus collaborates with frontal cortex and basal ganglia to implement the computations underlying voluntary decisions and action selection. One can conceptualize it as follows: cortex proposes, basal ganglia disposes, and thalamus gates the disposition back to cortex for execution. In computational terms, the thalamo-cortical loop in decisions might compute a "commitment function" - holding cortical plans in check until a threshold is met, then allowing full activation once the decision is made, thereby ensuring a definitive rather than wavering response.

AGI Design Principles

Forward-model separation. Cerebellar loops highlight the value of maintaining a parallel supervised simulator that learns dynamics rapidly and hands predictions to the slower policy network. In practice, this argues for a lightweight system-identification module sitting alongside a heavier policy/value learner.

Offline generative rehearsal. Hippocampal loops demonstrate how experience replay can be context-dependent, compositional and goal-directed, not just random sampling. Incorporating a replay controller that triggers targeted roll-outs when expected value of information is high can dramatically cut sample complexity.

Hierarchical gating rather than monolithic back-propagation. BG-style loops show how action and memory updates can be gated by local reinforcement signals without global credit transport. An AGI architecture can approximate this with striatal-like sparse gating modules that decide when downstream subnetworks update.

Thalamic routing for dynamic modularity. Thalamus teaches us that routing traffic between expert subnetworks can itself be an active, trainable process. Attentional transformers and mixture-of-experts schemes are early steps; a fuller analogue would add a learned gating matrix that can switch entire cortical areas on-the-fly.

Attractor-based working memory. Embedding shallow recurrent attractor micro-loops inside a deep feed-forward backbone can give an AGI stable latent states without constant refresh traffic, reducing energy and enabling long-horizon temporal credit assignment.
